subtopic: Kohlberg social contract stage
subtype: Laws as agreements that serve people [Actor]
passage:
First week of term: The college in Pune announced a new rule: no students in the library after 8 p.m. Francis was furious. "Stupid rule. I'll just sneak in through the back." His friend Darshan shook his head.
Two weeks later: In the law-and-society elective, the professor asked why rules exist at all. Francis surprised himself. "To protect everyone. Safety, fairness. But if a rule doesn't do that, people should be able to change it."
A month later: Francis didn't sneak in. He collected signatures from night-shift students who worked days, wrote to the student council, and presented data at the open meeting: forty students needed late hours. The college extended library hours till ten, with a guard. Darshan grinned. "Better than climbing the wall."

qa.q: Until what time did the college extend library hours?
qa.a: The college extended library hours till ten, with a guard.

qa.q: How did Francis feel about the new rule at first, and how did that change?
qa.a: He was furious at first and wanted to sneak in, but later felt a steadier sense that rules should protect people and could be changed fairly.

qa.q: Which of Francis's steps show a fair way to change an unjust rule?
qa.a: Collecting signatures, writing to the student council and presenting data at an open meeting, instead of breaking the rule.

qa.q: How does Darshan see Francis's change of approach?
qa.a: Darshan is amused and pleased, saying it's better than climbing the wall.

grounding: Over a month, a student moves from wanting to break a rule to reasoning that laws protect everyone and changing an unfair one by fair means.

subtopic: Kohlberg social contract stage
subtype: Laws as agreements that serve people [Actor]
passage:
"Arnab, you think rules are for obeying or for breaking. Let me tell you what I learned at twenty.
I, Imran, your Nanu, was studying in Aligarh. The hostel had a rule: no women visitors, not even mothers, in the common room. My friend's mother travelled eight hours to see him and had to sit outside in the rain.
Some boys wanted to break the gate lock in protest. I was angry too. But I kept thinking, why do we have rules at all? To keep people safe and treat them fairly. This rule did neither.
So we wrote a petition, met the warden, and took it to the university council. It took four months. The rule changed.
Rules are agreements, beta. When they stop serving people, you change them properly. You don't just smash the gate."

qa.q: How long did it take to change the hostel rule?
qa.a: It took four months.

qa.q: How did young Imran feel when his friend's mother had to sit outside in the rain?
qa.a: He felt angry and upset at the unfairness, like the boys who wanted to break the lock.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Imran's story, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Choosing a petition, the warden and the council over breaking the gate lock; it changed the rule through a fair process.

qa.q: How might the friend's mother have felt sitting outside in the rain?
qa.a: She probably felt humiliated and tired after travelling eight hours to see her son.

grounding: An elder recalls reasoning as a student that rules exist to protect people, and changing an unfair hostel rule by fair means.

subtopic: Kohlberg social contract stage
subtype: Laws as agreements that serve people [Actor]
passage:
The exam was in three days, and the new rule appeared on the notice board overnight: students who missed two lab sessions would be barred from the practical exam, no exceptions. Harish had missed two because of dengue, with a medical certificate.
His classmate Sarita was also caught. "Let's just forge the attendance register," someone in the corridor whispered.
Harish felt his stomach turn. "No. The rule is meant to make sure people learn the labs. It's not meant to punish sick people."
With little time and the head of department away, Harish and Sarita wrote a formal appeal, attached certificates and emailed it to the exam committee, copying the student representative. They also offered to do a make-up lab.
The committee met the next day. The rule was amended to allow medical exceptions.

qa.q: Why had Harish missed two lab sessions?
qa.a: Because of dengue, with a medical certificate.

qa.q: What was Harish feeling when someone suggested forging the register?
qa.a: He felt uneasy, his stomach turning, because breaking the rule felt wrong even though the rule was unfair.

qa.q: Why was the formal appeal a better choice than forging the register?
qa.a: It used a fair process that respected the rule's purpose and got it changed for everyone, without dishonesty.

qa.q: How might Sarita have felt about Harish's approach?
qa.a: Sarita probably felt relieved to have a fair way through, since she was also caught by the rule.

grounding: Under time pressure, a student reasons that a rule should serve students' welfare and changes an unfair one through a formal appeal.

subtopic: Kohlberg social contract stage
passage:
"You asked what the hardest part of being a young nurse is. I'm Usha, and it's this.
At our Shillong hospital, visiting hours end at seven. I follow that rule. Most nights it helps patients rest.
But one night, an old man was dying and his daughter, Lalremsiami, arrived from Guwahati at eight. The guard said no. I could have sneaked her in. Instead I called the duty doctor and filed an exception request. It was approved in ten minutes.
Afterward I wrote to the nursing board asking for a written exception for dying patients. They refused. Said it was too open to misuse.
I was disappointed. I still think they're wrong. But the process was fair. They heard me, gave reasons. So I follow it, and I'll raise it again next year."

qa.q: What time do visiting hours end at Usha's hospital?
qa.a: Visiting hours end at seven.

qa.q: How does Usha feel about the nursing board's refusal?
qa.a: Usha is disappointed and still thinks they're wrong, but accepts it because the process was fair.

qa.q: What does Usha's handling of the rule show?
qa.a: Follow rules in ordinary cases, use formal exceptions when a rule would cause harm, and accept a fair outcome while planning to raise it again.

qa.q: How might Lalremsiami have felt when the exception was approved?
qa.a: She likely felt deeply relieved and grateful to see her dying father.

grounding: A nurse follows the visiting rule normally, raises a formal objection when it would harm people, and accepts the fair outcome.

subtopic: Kohlberg social contract stage
passage:
Monday: Wasim, a junior engineer at a Chennai construction firm, got a new rule: all site workers must finish shifts by 6 p.m., even if the concrete pour was incomplete. He followed it, even when it meant redoing work.
Wednesday: A storm was coming. Stopping at six would leave wet concrete exposed and weaken the new floor, putting future residents at risk. Wasim wrote a formal objection to the site manager, Sarita, and asked for a one-time extension with safety lights and double crew breaks.
Friday: Sarita refused, citing labour-hour limits. Wasim felt frustrated. But she explained her reasons in writing and promised to review the policy with the safety team. Wasim covered the slab with tarpaulins and accepted the decision.

qa.q: What did Wasim use to cover the slab?
qa.a: He covered it with tarpaulins.

qa.q: How did Wasim feel when Sarita refused the extension?
qa.a: He felt frustrated but accepted it because Sarita gave reasons and promised a review.

qa.q: What was wise about how Wasim raised his concern?
qa.a: He followed the rule in ordinary cases, raised a formal objection with a safety plan when it could harm people, and accepted the fair decision.

qa.q: How does Sarita see the rule and Wasim's request?
qa.a: She has to balance workers' hour limits against the floor, and takes Wasim's objection seriously by explaining and promising a review.

grounding: An engineer follows a shift rule, formally objects when it would harm people, and accepts the fair outcome even when it goes against him.

subtopic: Kohlberg social contract stage
passage:
"Gautam, you asked how I handled the rules in my first job. Your Dadaji will tell you.
I, Vijay, was twenty-five, a clerk at the ration office in Nagpur. The rule was that no one could get rations without an ID card. I followed it every day.
Then a widow came, her card lost in a house fire. She had three children and nothing to eat.
I didn't just hand her rice under the table. I wrote to the district supply officer, explaining the case and asking for a temporary exception. My senior said I was wasting time.
The officer refused. The rule was the rule, he said, but he sent her to a relief shelter the same day and started a faster card replacement.
I was angry for a week. But I accepted it. The process was fair, and it helped her in another way."

qa.q: What had the widow lost in the house fire?
qa.a: She had lost her ID card.

qa.q: How did young Vijay feel after the officer refused?
qa.a: He was angry for a week, but accepted the decision because the process was fair and still helped her.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Vijay chose to write to the district officer instead of giving rice under the table, which led to relief for the widow and a faster card process.

qa.q: How might the widow have felt when she was sent to the relief shelter?
qa.a: She was likely relieved to get help for her children, even if it wasn't the rations she came for.

grounding: An elder recalls following a rule as a young clerk but formally raising an objection when it harmed a widow, and accepting the fair outcome.

subtopic: Kohlberg social contract stage
subtype: Person affected by a fair process feels respected [Receiver]
passage:
Mateo had complained to the Barcelona hotel's HR department that his shifts were always the late ones, while Rafael, who'd joined after him, got mornings.
He expected to be ignored. Instead, HR called both of them in, showed the shift records, and asked Mateo to explain. Then they explained: Rafael had a formal childcare arrangement approved last year, and seniority didn't decide mornings. They offered Mateo two morning shifts a month and a review in three months.
It wasn't what Mateo wanted. He'd hoped for half mornings.
But walking home, he felt oddly lighter. They had listened. They had shown him the records, given reasons, not just said no.
"I still don't love it," he told his sister. "But I trust them now."

qa.q: What did HR offer Mateo?
qa.a: Two morning shifts a month and a review in three months.

qa.q: How did Mateo feel walking home after the meeting?
qa.a: He felt oddly lighter and respected, even though he didn't get what he wanted, because they had listened and explained.

qa.q: What made the HR process fair in Mateo's eyes?
qa.a: They heard him, showed the shift records, explained the reasons openly and offered a review.

qa.q: How might Rafael have felt being called into the meeting?
qa.a: Rafael may have felt uneasy at first, but relieved that the reasons for his mornings were explained openly.

grounding: An employee whose complaint is heard, weighed openly and answered with reasons feels respected and trusts the system more, despite losing.

subtopic: Kohlberg social contract stage
subtype: Person affected by a fair process feels respected [Receiver]
passage:
At the Kolkata textile export office, Binita had filed a complaint that her promotion went to Imran, though she had more years in the team.
The panel met in the conference room. They let her speak first. They listened, asked questions, then shared the scoring sheet: Imran scored higher in the client-management test, which had been announced to all staff. They explained each point.
"We know this is disappointing," the chairperson said. "We'd like to offer you the client-management training so you're strong for the next round."
Binita's throat was tight. She had wanted the post badly. But she noticed her hands were steady. Nobody had brushed her off.
That evening she told her mother, "I didn't win. But they treated me like I mattered. I'll try again."

qa.q: Which test did Imran score higher in?
qa.a: He scored higher in the client-management test.

qa.q: How did Binita feel after the panel meeting?
qa.a: She was disappointed, with a tight throat, but also respected and steady because the panel listened and explained.

qa.q: What could Binita do next, based on the panel's offer?
qa.a: Take the client-management training so she's stronger for the next promotion round.

qa.q: How might Imran feel knowing the process was explained openly?
qa.a: Imran might feel his promotion is seen as fair, which could make working with Binita less awkward.

grounding: An employee whose promotion complaint is heard, weighed openly and answered with reasons feels respected and trusts the system despite losing.

subtopic: Kohlberg social contract stage

Dear Rukmini,
You asked how the complaint went. Well, I lost. But I'm strangely okay.
I'd complained to the school management that the new teacher timetable gave me all the Saturday classes. The committee actually called me in. They let me speak for as long as I needed. They didn't give me what I asked for. But nobody rolled their eyes. The principal thanked me for raising it properly.
I came out feeling respected. And I trust the committee now, which I didn't before.

Jaya

subtopic: Kohlberg social contract stage
passage:
I'm Tanuja, and I used to think that people who objected at work were either troublemakers or suck-ups. Then I watched Madhav.
Our call centre in Bengaluru brought in a policy: no toilet breaks outside the fixed two slots. Everyone grumbled in the canteen. Some people started faking system errors to get a break.
Madhav didn't grumble or fake anything. He wrote a calm email to HR with facts: pregnant colleagues, people on medication, a health guideline. He asked for a meeting. He still followed the slots while waiting.
Two weeks later, HR changed the rule. Madhav never bragged. He still stayed back to help the team lead.
I realised you can be loyal to your workplace and still stand for what's right.

qa.q: What did some people fake to get a break?
qa.a: Some people started faking system errors.

qa.q: How did Tanuja's feelings about objecting at work change after watching Madhav?
qa.a: Tanuja moved from seeing objectors as troublemakers to feeling admiration, realising loyalty and principle can go together.

qa.q: What made Madhav's objection work?
qa.a: He used calm facts, went through HR, asked for a meeting, and kept following the rule while waiting.

qa.q: How might the pregnant colleagues have been affected by the rule change?
qa.a: They would likely feel relieved and cared for, able to take breaks when they needed.

grounding: A colleague watches a peer object calmly to an unfair break policy through proper channels and learns loyalty and principle can go together.

subtopic: Kohlberg social contract stage
passage:
Shift supervisor's note, warehouse, Nagpur

This month the company announced that anyone late by five minutes would lose a full day's pay. Several workers were angry and one talked of blocking the loading bay.
Kiran, the other shift supervisor, did something different. She collected data on bus delays from the new ring road, met the operations head, and proposed a fair grace period with warnings. She kept enforcing the current rule on her shift while waiting.
I was surprised. I'd assumed Kiran would either stay silent to please management or side with the protesters. Eshaan, a new loader, asked me why she bothered. I said, "Because she believes in the rules, and in fixing them."
The policy was changed to a warning system last week.

qa.q: What did Kiran propose to the operations head?
qa.a: She proposed a fair grace period with warnings.

qa.q: Why did the note-writer feel surprised by Kiran?
qa.a: The note-writer felt surprised and impressed that Kiran neither stayed silent nor joined the protest, but objected through proper channels.

qa.q: Why did Kiran's approach work better than blocking the loading bay?
qa.a: She used data and a meeting, kept enforcing the rule meanwhile, and got the policy changed fairly without disrupting work.

qa.q: How might Eshaan see Kiran after the note-writer's answer?
qa.a: Eshaan may start seeing her as someone who respects rules and also works to make them fair.

grounding: A supervisor watches a peer object to an unfair lateness policy through proper channels and sees loyalty and principle together.

subtopic: Kohlberg social contract stage
passage:
Diary, Thursday

Saw something today I keep thinking about. Our bank branch got a new target: every customer must be pushed a credit card, even pensioners. Most of us just did it, grumbling. A couple of people started quietly skipping it and lying in the reports.
Tanuja didn't do either. She wrote to the regional manager with examples of elderly customers who were confused and upset, asked for an exemption for pensioners, and kept following the target for everyone else while she waited.
I, Saurabh, honestly thought she'd get in trouble. Instead the manager called her, thanked her, and the rule was changed yesterday.
She's still the first one in and the last one out. Loyal and principled. I didn't know you could be both.

subtopic: Kohlberg social contract stage
passage:
"You asked me how I handled the parking fight in our housing society. I'm Shankar, the secretary. Here's how.
The old rule said one car space per flat. But the ground-floor families had two elderly members with wheelchairs, and the new families had two cars each. Everyone was shouting on the group chat.
I called a meeting and wrote on a board: what's at stake? Safety for wheelchairs. Fairness between flats. Space for visitors. Then I asked each side to speak, three minutes each. Mohit, who usually stays quiet, spoke about his father's wheelchair. The room went silent.
We voted as the bylaws say. Accessible spots near the gate for anyone who needs them. Then we formed a small group to rewrite the parking rule properly by next year."

qa.q: How long did each side get to speak at the meeting?
qa.a: Three minutes each.

qa.q: Why did Shankar want each side to speak for three minutes?
qa.a: Shankar was worried the loudest voices would win and wanted everyone, even quiet residents, to feel heard and respected.

qa.q: What steps did Shankar take that made the process fair?
qa.a: He listed what was at stake, gave each side time to speak, followed the bylaws for the vote, and set up a group to improve the rule.

qa.q: What would change if the quieter residents like Mohit had not been invited to speak?
qa.a: The wheelchair users' needs might have been drowned out by the loudest voices.

grounding: An adult facing a parking rule conflict lays out what's at stake, invites people to speak, follows procedure and works to improve the rule.

subtopic: Kohlberg social contract stage
passage:
I'm Pooja. I work in the same school as Kavitha. I don't know what she was thinking inside, but here is what I saw.
The staff were split over a rule: no phones in class for teachers either. Some said it was unfair because they needed them for attendance. Others said teachers must set an example.
Kavitha, as staff coordinator, didn't pick a side. She wrote on the whiteboard: "Students' focus. Teachers' needs. Safety calls." She asked each teacher to speak, even the new ones who usually say nothing. She followed the procedure in the staff handbook and took a vote.
The rule stayed, with an exception for attendance and emergencies. Then she said, "Let's review it together in June." Nobody walked out angry. That's rare.

qa.q: What three things did Kavitha write on the whiteboard?
qa.a: Students' focus. Teachers' needs. Safety calls.

qa.q: What does Kavitha's choice not to pick a side suggest about her?
qa.a: It suggests she felt calm and fair-minded, wanting everyone's rights and welfare weighed, not just one group's.

qa.q: Which steps made Kavitha's process fair?
qa.a: Naming what was at stake, inviting every teacher to speak, following the handbook procedure, and planning a review.

qa.q: How might the new teachers have felt when Kavitha asked them to speak?
qa.a: They likely felt included and respected, perhaps for the first time in a staff meeting.

grounding: A colleague describes an adult handling a rule conflict by naming what's at stake, inviting voices, following procedure and planning improvement.

subtopic: Kohlberg social contract stage
passage:
March: Santosh, the new manager of a small bakery in Indore, found a problem. The old rule said staff got leave only in turn by seniority. But Harish's wife was in hospital, and he'd been refused because two seniors had booked leave first.
April: Santosh called a staff meeting. He listed what was at stake: fairness of the queue, care for a family emergency, the shop's needs. Each worker spoke. One senior offered to swap dates. They agreed by vote, as the staff rules allowed.
June: Santosh wrote a new clause with the staff: emergency leave outside the queue, with proof. Harish, back at work, said, "Nobody pushed anyone. That's why it worked."

qa.a: Because two seniors had booked leave first.

qa.q: How did Harish seem to feel about how the conflict was handled?
qa.a: He seemed grateful and respected, saying nobody pushed anyone.

qa.a: Writing a new emergency-leave clause with the staff after a fair meeting and vote.

qa.a: The senior probably felt good about helping, since it was an open choice, not something forced.

grounding: Over months, a manager handles a leave-rule conflict by naming what's at stake, hearing everyone, voting fairly and improving the rule.

It was Holi, and the colony park was full of coloured water. Gautam squirted Siddharth right in the face. Siddharth, five, raised his hand to hit him, then stopped.
"Why didn't you hit him?" his older cousin asked.
"Because hitting is bad," Siddharth said.
"Why is it bad?"
"Because Mumma will shout and I won't get gujiya." He said it like it was the same as saying the sky is blue.
He wiped his face with his sleeve and went to fill his own pichkari.

qa.a: He went to fill his own pichkari.

qa.q: Why did Siddharth stop himself from hitting Gautam?

qa.q: How could Siddharth's mother build on his answer?
qa.a: She could praise his stopping and gently add that hitting hurts people, so he starts thinking about others' feelings too.

qa.q: How might Gautam feel if Siddharth had hit him?
qa.a: Gautam would probably feel hurt and upset, and the Holi play might have turned into a fight.

grounding: A child stops himself from hitting because his mother will be angry, judging right by punishment.

subtopic: Kohlberg stages: contrast with other stages

"Shreya, why did you take the Christmas star back from Vijay?" asked the teacher at the playgroup party.
"Because he snatched it. Snatching is naughty."
"Why is snatching naughty?"
Shreya frowned. "Because Ma'am gets angry. And you go in the quiet corner."
"What if Ma'am wasn't looking?"
Shreya thought, eyes wide. "Then... it's still naughty. Because Ma'am might look."
The teacher smiled. "What about how Vijay feels?"

qa.a: Gently ask how Shreya felt when someone took her things, linking rules to feelings, not just punishment.

qa.a: Vijay probably just wanted the star and may feel upset that Shreya wants him in the quiet corner.

subtopic: Kohlberg stages: contrast with other stages

Nursery note, Eid week

Chetan (5) pushed Irfan off the swing today. When I asked him why pushing is wrong, he said, "Because you get a time-out." I asked, "Is it wrong if nobody sees?" He said, "Somebody always sees."
He could not say how Irfan felt, even though Irfan was crying. He only asked if he would miss the Eid sweets.
I sat with both boys and asked Irfan to show Chetan where it hurt. Chetan watched and said, "Sorry, sorry." I will keep pointing out feelings, not only rules.

qa.a: He said, "Because you get a time-out."

qa.q: What was Chetan worried about after pushing Irfan?
qa.a: He was worried about punishment, asking if he'd miss the Eid sweets, rather than about Irfan's feelings.

qa.q: What is the note-writer planning, and why does it help?
qa.a: To keep pointing out feelings, not only rules, so Chetan learns that pushing hurts people, not just that it earns time-outs.

qa.q: How might Irfan feel when Chetan says sorry?
qa.a: Irfan might feel a bit comforted, seeing Chetan notice where it hurt.

grounding: A nursery note shows a child who judges pushing as wrong only because of time-outs, and a teacher starting to point him to feelings.

subtopic: Kohlberg stages: contrast with other stages
passage:
Luca, sixteen, lived in Milan and was known as the "good son" and the loyal friend. He helped his parents at their café every weekend and never missed a friend's birthday.
When his friend group decided to skip the school trip and go to the lake instead, Luca felt his chest tighten. His parents had paid for the trip. His mother had told everyone how proud she was of him.
"You coming?" asked Valentina, his closest friend.
He wanted to. He didn't want to be the one who ruined the plan. But he couldn't bear his mother's face if she found out.
"I can't," he said finally. "My mum would be so disappointed."
Valentina rolled her eyes. "You always care what everyone thinks."
Luca went on the trip, and felt bad about his friends all day.

qa.q: Where did Luca help his parents every weekend?
qa.a: He helped at their café.

qa.q: What was Luca feeling when Valentina asked if he was coming?
qa.a: He felt torn and anxious, wanting his friends' approval but unable to bear disappointing his mother.

qa.q: What could Luca try so he isn't pulled apart by everyone's approval?
qa.a: Think about what he himself values, and explain calmly to friends and family, rather than choosing only by who might be disappointed.

qa.q: How does Valentina see Luca's choice?
qa.a: Valentina sees him as someone who always cares what everyone thinks, and is annoyed he won't join them.

grounding: A teenage boy acts to be seen as a good son and loyal friend, and finds it hard when their expectations clash.

subtopic: Kohlberg stages: contrast with other stages
passage:
In the school cricket club in Lucknow, Charan, fifteen, was everyone's favourite: dependable, polite, a good son who always carried his mother's bags at the market.
After practice, the team captain said, "We're going to tell Sir that Rohan broke the window, not us. Everyone agree?"
Charan knew it wasn't Rohan. His stomach twisted. But everyone was looking at him. If he said no, he'd be the traitor.
Salma, the club manager, noticed him hesitating. "Charan? You look pale."
"I don't want to let the team down," he said quietly.
"And what about Rohan?"
Charan's throat was tight. Being a good friend to the team and being a good person suddenly felt like two different things.

qa.q: Who did the captain want to blame for the broken window?
qa.a: The captain wanted to tell Sir that Rohan broke the window.

qa.q: What was Charan feeling when everyone looked at him?
qa.a: He felt his stomach twist, afraid of being the traitor and letting the team down, but uneasy about blaming Rohan.

qa.q: How could Salma help Charan through this?
qa.a: She could support him to tell the truth to the coach, and help the team own up together, so he doesn't have to choose between loyalty and honesty alone.

qa.q: How might Rohan feel if the team blamed him?
qa.a: Rohan would likely feel hurt and betrayed, blamed for something he didn't do.

grounding: A teenage boy who wants to be seen as a good friend and son finds it hard to go against the group, even when it's wrong.

subtopic: Kohlberg stages: contrast with other stages
passage:

I'm writing because I couldn't say it on the phone.
You asked why I didn't come to the concert with everyone on Saturday. The truth is, Papa asked me to stay home with Dadi because she wasn't well. I wanted to come so much. I kept thinking you'd all say I'm boring, that I never do anything fun.

In the small town of Hoshangabad, Irfan worked as a trainee at the municipal water office. He was known for following every rule to the letter.
When an old widow, Vidya Bai, came to ask for a water connection without the required land papers, which had been lost in a flood, Irfan shook his head.
"I'm sorry, Amma. No papers, no connection."
"But I've lived there forty years. Everyone knows it's my house."
Irfan felt a pang. But he said, "If I break the rule for you, what stops everyone breaking it? The whole system falls apart."
She walked away slowly. Irfan stood at the counter, feeling right and uneasy at once. That evening he looked up whether there was any official procedure for lost papers.

qa.q: What had Vidya Bai lost in a flood?
qa.a: She had lost her land papers.

qa.q: What was Irfan feeling as Vidya Bai walked away?
qa.a: He felt right and uneasy at once, believing in the rule but pained by its cost to her.

qa.q: What could Irfan do next to respect both order and Vidya Bai's need?
qa.a: Find and follow the official procedure for lost papers, or ask his senior about an approved exception process.

qa.q: How might Vidya Bai see the office's refusal?
qa.a: She likely feels hurt and unfairly treated, since everyone knows she has lived there forty years.

grounding: A young official treats rules as holding society together, which supports order but is hard on a widow facing a rare exception.

Layla, twenty, was a student volunteer marshal at the Leeds half marathon. The rule was clear: no one could cross the course while runners were passing.
An old man with shopping bags wanted to cross to reach his bus. "Please, love, it's just there."
"I'm sorry, sir. If I let you, then everyone will want to cross. It could cause an accident."
Her friend Amara, marshalling beside her, whispered, "He's going to miss his bus. There's a gap now."
Layla's cheeks were hot. "Rules keep people safe. That's the point."
The old man sighed and waited. Layla felt proud of holding the line, and a bit sick watching his bus pull away.
When the course cleared, she walked him to the next stop herself.

qa.a: She felt proud of holding the line but also a bit sick about the cost to him.

qa.q: What did Layla do afterward that softened the rule's harshness?
qa.a: She walked him to the next stop herself once the course cleared.

qa.q: How does Amara see the situation differently?
qa.a: Amara sees a safe gap and the man's need, and thinks the rule could bend this once.

grounding: A young adult treats rules as keeping order and safety for all, which is hard on an old man facing a small, rare exception.

Ethics tutor's note, second-year psychology

Tenzin gave two very different answers this week. In Monday's debate about exam cheating, he said, "It's wrong because you'll be caught and expelled." That is simple, punishment-based reasoning.
On Thursday, discussing a case about a nurse who broke a hospital rule to save a patient, he argued carefully about human dignity and when rules should give way.
Gurleen joked afterward, "So which stage is Tenzin, low or high?"
I explained that the stages are patterns in how reasoning develops, not scores for people. The same person can reason at different levels depending on the situation, stress, or how close the issue feels. Tenzin looked relieved. I've asked the class to notice this in their own answers.

qa.q: What did Tenzin say about exam cheating on Monday?
qa.a: He said it's wrong because you'll be caught and expelled.

qa.q: What did the note-writer want Gurleen and the class to understand?
qa.a: The note-writer was concerned they'd rank people, and wanted them to see stages as patterns of reasoning that vary by situation.

qa.q: Why is it useful to see the stages as tendencies rather than labels?
qa.a: It helps students see how reasoning grows and changes with context, instead of judging who is a better person.

qa.q: How might Tenzin feel when Gurleen jokes about his stage?
qa.a: He might feel embarrassed or judged, and then relieved when the tutor explains stages aren't labels.

grounding: A tutor notices the same student reasoning at different levels and treats the stages as patterns of growth, not a ranking of people.

Something from today's college ethics class that I want to remember as a new lecturer.

"You want to know why I left the company? I'm Raghav. I was a junior engineer at a chemical plant.
